title: Family asks why relative had to die: Police service's shoot-to-kill policy criticized
article: Family and friends of Deng Fermino Kuol -- shot dead early Saturday by a Calgary police officer he attacked with a knife -- want to know why the officer shot to kill.
The incident has also prompted the president of the Alberta Civil Liberties Association to call for the creation of an independent body to investigate such incidents.
Meanwhile, those who work with the city's Sudanese population fear the fatal shooting will destroy progress made in this area.
Stephen Jenuth, president of the civil liberties association, argues it is "very rare" for an internal police investigation to reveal misconduct.

"The situation we have now . . . makes it very unlikely that police misconduct ever gets found," said Jenuth. "And with the cases where it is found, it has to be so egregious that it just can't go unpunished."
Akwoch Ding, a friend of Kuol's for five years, is calling for the provincial government to intervene in the investigation and to change the way police handle such situations.
"We are really very sad and we feel like something has to be done by the government. The police has to be reformed," said Ding.
Kuol's cousin Akon Malou voiced disapproval of the police service's policy that officers should shoot to kill aggressors.
"He should have shot him in the leg or the arm," said Malou.
She added that "police have a lot of things to use" in subduing attackers, pointing to batons and pepper spray as examples.
Piot Dol, a friend of Kuol's, added that if the officer couldn't get Kuol to leave the building, he should have called for backup.
Const. Ira Macumber responded to a call to remove Kuol, 34, from a building at 1709 37th St. S.E. shortly after 12:30 a.m. Saturday.
Kuol, who was unemployed and homeless after being laid off from Lakeside Packers in Brooks earlier this year, was sitting outside the residence when Macumber arrived.
Investigators said after initially agreeing to leave, Kuol drew a knife and slashed the officer in the left bicep.
Macumber struggled to restrain his attacker, then pulled his gun and fired twice -- in keeping with police training.
Officers are taught to aim at aggressors' central body mass, said police.
Kuol's family and friends, who gathered Sunday afternoon in southeast Calgary to console each other, dispute Kuol had a knife during the incident and say he wasn't a violent person.
"He never carried a knife in his life," said Ding.
Added Malou: "He doesn't like to fight with people."
Kuol's younger brother, Bol Agot, 24, travelled from Brooks to attend the congregation of the Sudanese community, which attracted about 50 people.
Agot described his brother as an "honest" person who had many friends.
But Staff Sgt. Barry Cochrane of the Calgary homicide unit defends the police's initial findings that Kuol drew a knife on Macumber.
"From our investigation, the knife was produced by the subject and used against the officer. The struggle was to take control of that knife, which resulted in the shooting," said Cochrane.
Homicide investigators are now trying to determine if Macumber was justified in using deadly force to subdue Kuol.

Police officers around the country are trained to respond with deadly force if they fear "death or grievous bodily harm" to themselves or the public, according to a Calgary weapons and self- defence expert.
Paul McDougall, the manager of the Calgary Rifle and Pistol Club, says officers are taught to withhold such measures unless other methods have failed and someone's life is in danger.

"If a subject is within 20 feet and aggressive with a knife, you are in danger of being stabbed," said McDougall, who has been a special constable in Turner Valley, Black Diamond and Cochrane, and remains in the law-enforcement industry as a consultant.
"He can get you before you can shoot him," he said.

Edna Sutherland, the executive director of the Calgary Immigrant Women's Association, said Calgary's Sudanese community, which has grown over the past five years from 500 to 7,500, is under stress because they come from a war-torn country.
Sutherland is concerned how the group will react to the shooting death of one of their own in a country they perceive as safe.
"We've made some good progress on the relationship with the police -- a reduction in violence and a reduction of many issues," said Sutherland. "I want to make sure that that's not undermined."
